title: Nanoscape: The Journal for Undergraduate Research in Nanoscience
description: Nanoscape: The Journal for Undergraduate Research in Nanoscience is an annual publication of original research conducted by undergraduates from around the county. The journal was launched in 2004 and was the first of its kind in the country. The journal disseminates the results of undergraduate research in the broad fields of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Nanoscape is an educational outreach project of the Northwestern University Nanoscale Science and Engineering Center (NSEC), which is part of the International Institute for Nanotechnology (IIN), both of which are under the direction of Professor Chad A. Mirkin. This work was supported primarily by the Nanoscale Science and Engineering Initiative of the National Science Foundation Under NSF award number EEC–0755375 AND EEC-0647560.

title: Patterning of BaTiO3 Nanostructures Using Modified Micromolding in Capillaries
creator: Vinayak P. Dravid
Jesse Hall III
Zixiao Pan
description:
There is a continuing need for patterning
multifunctional materials to harness their
features and explore synergy among
diverse properties and phenomena. Soft
lithography, among various patterning
techniques, is a versatile method that can
generate inorganic patterns in a parallel
mode. Experimentation was performed
making use of flexible soft lithography to
fabricate miniature patterns of a complex
multifunctional oxide, BaTiO3. Specifically,
a modified method of micromolding in
capillaries (MIMIC) was used with solbased
starting materials. Modifications of
MIMIC consisted of an O2 plasma treatment
to the surface of the mold and substrate
and the use of a thin-film mold. Nanoscale
features (~ 50nm) were produced with this
modified method and examined using
atomic force microscopy (AFM) and
scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The
patterns were found to be highly dense,
uniform, and continuous over a relatively
large area. These modifications to the
traditional MIMIC technique were
significant; the resulting method proved to
be simple and effective in producing the
desired patterns.
